clinicalPearls: A rare tumour of intermediate biological potential that usually arises in the superficial soft tissue of the extremities in children and young adults

Classic histology shows nodules of bland ovoid to spindled histiocytoid cells, blood-filled pseudoangiomatous cystic spaces, a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and a peripheral cuff of lymphoid tissue that can mimic a lymph node
May cause systemic symptoms such as fever, anaemia, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers, thought to be cytokine-mediated and reversible after resection
Most cases harbour an EWSR1-CREB1 fusion; less commonly EWSR1-ATF1 or FUS-ATF1
Immunophenotype is variable but often includes desmin, EMA, CD68 and CD99, with absence of specific melanocytic, vascular and myogenic differentiation
The blood-filled spaces are pseudovascular and not lined by endothelium, distinguishing it from a true vascular tumour
Despite the historical name, it is not a fibrohistiocytic malignancy and only rarely metastasises
reference.pathophysiology: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is defined by a recurrent gene fusion, most often EWSR1-CREB1, in which the EWSR1 gene is joined to a CREB-family transcription-factor gene, activating aberrant transcriptional programmes that drive proliferation and may promote cytokine production responsible for systemic symptoms. The lesion forms circumscribed nodules with pseudoangiomatous haemorrhagic spaces, a fibrous pseudocapsule and a lymphoid cuff. The same fusions occur in certain other tumours, so integration of morphology, immunophenotype and molecular findings is needed for a confident diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Nodal metastasis or a reactive lymph node, given the lymphoid cuff
Vascular tumours such as haemangioma and angiosarcoma
Other EWSR1-rearranged tumours including clear cell sarcoma and myoepithelioma
additionalInvestigations: Immunohistochemistry for desmin, EMA, CD68 and CD99 with exclusion of endothelial and melanocytic markers
FISH or molecular testing for EWSR1 (and ATF1/CREB1) or FUS rearrangement
Endothelial markers (CD31, ERG) to confirm the pseudovascular spaces lack a true endothelial lining
Blood count and inflammatory markers to document reversible systemic effects
MRI to characterise the superficial soft-tissue mass
Complete excision specimen assessment for margins and depth of invasion
redFlags: Deep, large or infiltrative tumours, which have a higher risk of aggressive behaviour
Rare distant metastasis, most often to lymph nodes and lung
Persistent systemic inflammatory symptoms suggesting incomplete resection
reference.prognosis: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is generally cured by complete excision and has an excellent overall prognosis, with local recurrence in a minority and metastasis in only a small percentage of cases; deep or truncal tumours with infiltrative margins carry the greatest risk, and any accompanying systemic symptoms usually resolve once the tumour is removed.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the lymphoid cuff as a lymph node and diagnosing metastatic disease
Mistaking the pseudovascular spaces for a true vascular tumour
Overlooking the diagnosis because the immunophenotype is variable and non-specific
Failing to attribute unexplained fever and anaemia to the tumour
Assuming the EWSR1 rearrangement indicates Ewing sarcoma or clear cell sarcoma

management: AFH is classified as an intermediate, rarely metastasising soft tissue tumour, so it is managed primarily as a local-control problem rather than one routinely needing systemic therapy
Complete surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment and is curative in most patients
Biopsy should aim for molecular confirmation of an EWSR1 or FUS rearrangement to secure the diagnosis and exclude aggressive mimics such as Ewing sarcoma or clear cell sarcoma
Adjuvant radiotherapy is not routine but should be considered when margins are incomplete or infiltrative, or when the tumour is deep or truncal
If initial excision is incomplete, re-excision to achieve clear margins is the preferred next step when feasible
Radiotherapy can be used as an adjunct when further surgery would be excessively morbid or margins remain compromised
Distant metastasis is rare and, when it occurs, is most often nodal or pulmonary
There is no established systemic regimen specific to metastatic AFH, so any systemic therapy decision should be individualized through a sarcoma multidisciplinary tumour board
Systemic sarcoma chemotherapy regimens used for high grade sarcomas should not be extrapolated to AFH without multidisciplinary discussion, given its more favorable biology
AFH can cause cytokine mediated systemic symptoms such as fever, anaemia, weight loss, and raised inflammatory markers, which typically resolve after complete resection
Persistence of systemic symptoms after surgery should prompt evaluation for residual or incompletely excised tumour
Long-term follow-up focuses on local recurrence and, to a lesser extent, distant metastasis risk, which is highest with deep or infiltrative lesions
Surveillance should include clinical follow-up of the resection site with imaging if recurrence is clinically suspected, following general soft tissue tumour follow-up practice
Refer to a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team for surgical planning when disease is deep, large, truncal, incompletely excised, or metastatic
